2-5.title: Being Kind
2-5.description: Sharing, helping, and saying sorry. How to be a good friend.

en.title: Being Kind
en.welcome: Do you want to be a Superhero? The best superpower is Kindness! Zap! You made someone smile!
en.mainContent:
**Sharing:**
*   If you have two cookies, and your friend has none... what do you do?
*   Share! It makes your friend happy. And it makes YOU happy too!

**Helping:**
*   Oh no! Mommy dropped her keys. 
*   Pick them up! 'Here you go, Mommy.'
*   Helping hands are happy hands.

**Saying Sorry:**
*   Oops! Did you bump into someone? Bonk!
*   Say 'I'm sorry.' It fixes the ouchie inside.
*   Ask 'Are you okay?'

**The Golden Rule:**
*   Treat others how YOU want to be treated.
*   Do you like to be hit? No! So don't hit.
*   Do you like hugs? Yes! So give hugs (if they want one).

**Feelings:**
*   When you are kind, your heart feels warm and fuzzy.
*   When you are mean, your tummy feels yucky.
keyPoints: Sharing makes everyone happy
Helping is a superpower
Saying Sorry fixes mistakes
The Golden Rule: Treat others nicely
Kindness feels good inside
interactionPrompts: Show me your 'Helping Hands'. Wiggle them!
If your friend is sad, what can you do?
Practice saying 'I'm sorry' in a nice voice.
en.wisdomMoment: Kindness is like a boomerang. If you throw it, it comes back to you!
en.cta: Do one kind thing today. Draw a picture for someone. Share a toy. Be a hero.
en.summary: You learned about Sharing, Helping, Saying Sorry, The Golden Rule, and Warm Fuzzies!

6-12.title: Ethics: Right vs. Wrong
6-12.description: Dilemmas, fairness, and how to decide

en.title: Ethics: Right vs. Wrong
en.welcome: Is it ever okay to lie? What if it's to save a friend? Ethics is the study of these hard questions. It's the compass for your life.
en.mainContent:
**The Golden Rule:** Treat others how you want to be treated. It's in almost every religion and culture. It's the first rule of Ethics.

**Intent vs. Outcome:**
*   **Intent:** Did you *mean* to do good? (You tried to help but broke a vase. Are you bad? No).
*   **Outcome:** What actually happened? (The vase is broken).
*   Most people think Intent matters more for kids!

**The Trolley Problem (Simplified):** 
*   A runaway train is heading for 5 people.
*   You can pull a lever to switch tracks, but it will hit 1 person.
*   What do you do? Do nothing (5 hurt) or Act (1 hurt)? 
*   There is no 'right' answer! It shows that ethics is tricky.

**Fairness:**
*   **Equality:** Everyone gets the same (1 cookie each).
*   **Equity:** Everyone gets what they *need* (The hungry kid gets 2 cookies).

**Character:** Who are you when no one is looking? That is your character. Being honest, brave, and kind builds a strong character.
keyPoints: The Golden Rule is the foundation of ethics
Intent (Meaning to) vs. Outcome (What happened)
Ethical Dilemmas (Trolley Problem) have no easy answers
Equality (Same) vs. Equity (Fair)
Character is who you are in the dark
interactionPrompts: If you found a wallet with money, what would you do?
Is it okay to steal bread to feed a hungry family? (The Aladdin question)
Would you pull the lever in the Trolley Problem?
en.wisdomMoment: Wrong is wrong even if everyone is doing it. Right is right even if no one is doing it. (St. Augustine). Be brave enough to stand alone.
en.cta: Write down 3 words you want people to say about you (e.g., Kind, Honest, Funny). That is your goal.
en.summary: You've explored The Golden Rule, Intent vs. Outcome, Trolley Problem, Fairness, and Character.

en.title: Moral Philosophy: How to Decide
en.welcome: When you have a tough choice, how do you decide? Philosophers have argued about this for 2,000 years. Here are the three main schools of thought.
en.mainContent:
**1. Utilitarianism (The Outcome):** 
*   *Idea:* The greatest good for the greatest number.
*   *Focus:* Consequences.
*   *Example:* Killing 1 person to save 5 is GOOD because 5 > 1.
*   *Problem:* Can justify terrible things (slavery?) if it helps the majority.

**2. Deontology (The Rules):** 
*   *Idea:* Some things are just wrong, no matter what. (Kant).
*   *Focus:* Duty/Rules.
*   *Example:* Killing is WRONG. Period. Even to save 5 people. You cannot use a person as a tool.
*   *Problem:* Can be too rigid. (You can't lie to a murderer to save your friend?).

**3. Virtue Ethics (The Character):** 
*   *Idea:* Focus on being a good person (Aristotle).
*   *Focus:* Habits/Character.
*   *Example:* What would a virtuous person (like Superman or Jesus) do? Act like them.
*   *Goal:* Eudaimonia (Flourishing).

**The Veil of Ignorance (Rawls):** How to design a fair society? Imagine you don't know who you will be (Rich/Poor, Healthy/Sick). You would design a society that is fair for everyone, just in case you end up at the bottom.
keyPoints: Utilitarianism: Focus on Results (Greatest Good)
Deontology: Focus on Rules (Duty)
Virtue Ethics: Focus on Character (Being Good)
Veil of Ignorance: A tool for fairness
Different situations might require different frameworks
interactionPrompts: Which framework do you like best? (Results, Rules, or Character?)
Apply the 'Veil of Ignorance' to your school. Is it fair?
Is it ever okay to break a rule to do the right thing?
en.wisdomMoment: Character is destiny. (Heraclitus). Who you are determines what you do.
en.core_metaphor: Three lenses for viewing the world
en.cta: Think of a recent choice. Did you make it based on Rules, Results, or Character?
en.summary: You've explored Utilitarianism, Deontology, Virtue Ethics, and The Veil of Ignorance.

18-35.title: Applied Ethics: Bioethics and AI
18-35.description: Modern dilemmas: Gene editing, AI rights, and environmental ethics

en.title: Applied Ethics: Bioethics and AI
en.welcome: Technology moves fast. Ethics moves slow. We are creating gods (AI, CRISPR) without the wisdom to handle them. Let's apply philosophy to the future.
en.mainContent:
**Bioethics (CRISPR):** We can edit DNA. 
*   *Therapy:* Curing cancer? Yes, please.
*   *Enhancement:* Making babies smarter/taller? This creates a genetic caste system (Gattaca). Is it fair?

**AI Ethics:** 
*   *The Alignment Problem:* How do we ensure AI wants what we want? (Paperclip Maximizer: AI destroys the world to make more paperclips).
*   *Bias:* AI learns from the internet. The internet is racist/sexist. Therefore, AI is racist/sexist. How do we fix the data?
*   *Rights:* If an AI becomes conscious, does it have rights? Is turning it off murder?

**Environmental Ethics:** 
*   *Anthropocentrism:* Protecting nature for humans.
*   *Biocentrism:* Protecting nature for itself. Do trees have rights? (Legal personhood for rivers).

**The Trolley Problem 2.0 (Self-Driving Cars):** 
*   A self-driving car must crash. Should it kill the pedestrian or the passenger? We have to code the ethics into the machine.

**Effective Altruism:** Using logic to do the most good. 
*   Is it better to donate to a local art museum or a malaria net charity? EA says malaria nets save more lives per dollar. It challenges our emotional giving.
keyPoints: Technology outpaces ethics (The Collingridge Dilemma)
Bioethics: Therapy vs. Enhancement
AI Ethics: Alignment, Bias, and Rights
Environmental Ethics: Do non-humans have rights?
Self-Driving Cars force us to code morality
Effective Altruism: Maximizing impact

en.wisdomMoment: With great power comes great responsibility. (Stan Lee / Voltaire). We are wielding the power of gods.
en.core_metaphor: Ethics is the steering wheel for technology
en.cta: Read about the 'Trolley Problem' for self-driving cars (The Moral Machine). Take the quiz online.

36-60.title: Everyday Ethics: Integrity in Action
36-60.description: Workplace ethics, white lies, and moral courage

en.title: Everyday Ethics: Integrity in Action
en.welcome: Ethics isn't just for trolley problems. It's for Tuesday mornings. It's about the small choices we make every day that define who we are.
en.mainContent:
**Integrity:** Doing the right thing when no one is watching. 
*   *Example:* Returning the extra change the cashier gave you. Not taking credit for someone else's work.

**White Lies:** Are they okay? 
*   *Pro:* They spare feelings ('I love your haircut').
*   *Con:* They erode trust. If you lie about small things, will you lie about big things? (The Slippery Slope).
*   *Radical Honesty:* Telling the truth, but with kindness.

**Workplace Ethics:** 
*   *Whistleblowing:* Reporting bad behavior (fraud, harassment). It takes immense courage. You might lose your job, but you keep your soul.
*   *Gossip:* It bonds people, but it destroys culture. Be the person who stops the gossip chain.

**Moral Courage:** It's easy to be good when it's easy. It's hard to be good when it costs you something (money, popularity, safety). This is where heroes are made.

**The Eulogy Test (David Brooks):** There are 'Resume Virtues' (Skills, Success) and 'Eulogy Virtues' (Kindness, Honesty, Love). We spend all our time on the Resume, but we want to be remembered for the Eulogy. Focus on the Eulogy.
keyPoints: Integrity is consistency of character
White Lies can erode trust over time
Whistleblowing requires Moral Courage
Gossip destroys community
Focus on Eulogy Virtues (Character) over Resume Virtues (Success)
interactionPrompts: When was the last time you told a 'White Lie'? Why?
Have you ever stood up for someone when it was scary?
What do you want written in your Eulogy?
en.wisdomMoment: The time is always right to do what is right. (MLK). Don't wait.
en.cta: Practice 'Radical Honesty' today. If you don't want to go to a party, don't say you are sick. Say 'I need some rest.'
en.summary: You've explored Integrity, White Lies, Workplace Ethics, Moral Courage, and The Eulogy Test.

61-102.title: The Examined Life: Ethics for Elders
61-102.description: Regret, forgiveness, and passing on values

en.title: The Examined Life: Ethics for Elders
en.welcome: Socrates said, 'The unexamined life is not worth living.' In the final chapters, we look back. We judge our own lives. This is the ultimate ethical audit.
en.mainContent:
**Regret:** The Top 5 Regrets of the Dying (Bronnie Ware): 
1.  I wish I'd had the courage to live a life true to myself.
2.  I wish I hadn't worked so hard.
3.  I wish I'd had the courage to express my feelings.
4.  I wish I had stayed in touch with my friends.
5.  I wish I had let myself be happier.
*   *Lesson:* It's not too late to fix these.

**Forgiveness:** Holding a grudge is like drinking poison and expecting the other person to die. Forgiveness is not for them; it is for YOU. It frees you from the past.

**Ethical Wills:** A legal will leaves your money. An Ethical Will leaves your values. Write a letter to your family sharing what you learned about life, love, and integrity.

**Wisdom:** Wisdom is knowledge + experience + ethics. You have seen the consequences of bad choices. You can warn the next generation (even if they don't listen!).

**Peace:** A good conscience is a soft pillow. If you have lived with integrity, you can rest easy. If not, you can make amends now.
keyPoints: The Unexamined Life is not worth living
Top Regrets: Authenticity, Work, Feelings, Friends, Happiness
Forgiveness is essential for peace
Ethical Wills pass on values, not just valuables
A good conscience brings peace at the end
interactionPrompts: Do you have any of the 'Top 5 Regrets'?
Is there anyone you need to forgive? (Including yourself?)
What is the most important value you want to pass on?
en.wisdomMoment: In the end, only three things matter: how much you loved, how gently you lived, and how gracefully you let go of things not meant for you. (Buddha).
en.core_metaphor: Life is a book; this is the conclusion
en.cta: Start writing your 'Ethical Will.' Just one paragraph. 'I want my grandchildren to know that...'
en.summary: You've explored The Examined Life, Top 5 Regrets, Forgiveness, Ethical Wills, Wisdom, and Peace.
